newsitem.title: USA: Final CME live hog deliveries attract scant notice.
newsitem.headline: Final CME live hog deliveries attract scant notice.

text.p: The last physical deliveries of live hogs against Chicago Mercantile Exchange futures -- 27 loads against the December contract -- went almost unnoticed on Monday, industry sources said.
"I would say the prevailing feeling among most people is 'good riddance'" to the delivery system, said Chuck Levitt, a livestock analyst with Alaron Trading Corp in Chicago.
Difficulties in finding hogs that met CME specifications in recent years, coupled with packer competition, often inflated cash terminal prices during delivery, Levitt said.
Changes in packer buying practices to pricing carcasses based on lean meat content, rather than basing prices solely on the weight of the live hog, spurred changes in the contract a year ago.

Consumer preference for lean pork had led to adjustments in the way meat packers bought hogs, according to industry sources. Packers rewarded producers who sold lean hogs by paying premiums based on fat measurements at the plant and penalized producers who sold fat hogs by heavy discounting.

A National Pork Producers Council study in 1993 noted the surge in carcass-based pricing. The study found that nearly 74 percent of all hogs bought were on a grade and yield basis, compared with only 14 percent in 1984.
Lean hog futures were first listed November 10, 1995 as the February 1997 contract, replacing a delivery system established in 1966, CME officials said.

The new contract represents 40,000 pounds of hog carcasses compared with 40,000 pounds of live hogs under the old contract. Open positions at expiration will be closed with cash settlement instead of actual hog deliveries.
"We went modern," Levitt said. "This new contract makes it easier for producers to hedge and makes it easier for international investors to trade," Levitt said.
Reaction in the country to the phasing out of physical hog deliveries was subdued.
"I don't think anyone will miss it," said a hog buyer in southern Minnesota. "There hasn't been much comment."
